artworks.title: Heliades
artworks.description: Bunny’s Symbolist canvas gathers Phaethon’s sisters in a dusk of gold and mourning — bodies already half-poplar, amber tears implied in the palette. Painted in Paris for the fin-de-siècle taste for Ovidian metamorphosis, it is among the few modern pictures that name the Heliades as the subject rather than their brother’s fall alone.

artworks.title: The Sisters of Phaethon Transformed into Poplars
artworks.description: An Ovidian plate freezes the sisters mid-change: bark climbing limbs, arms still raised in lament for Phaethon. The print tradition made the Heliades’ poplars and amber tears a standard Metamorphoses vignette for European readers who knew the sun-god’s daughters chiefly through that Latin grief.

artworks.title: The Sisters of Phaethon
artworks.description: Santi di Tito’s Mannerist scene stages the Heliades’ transformation on the Eridanus bank — sisters turning to trees while the river and mourning gods close the myth of Phaethon’s fall. Florentine disegno keeps the Oceanid daughters visible as a chorus of grief before the bark seals them.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses II (Phaethon)
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Ovid’s Phaethon book ends with the Heliades weeping amber beside the Eridanus — the Latin source that fixed their poplar metamorphosis for later art and schoolrooms.
